Subordinate

/suh-BOR-dih-nit/ - the stress falls on BOR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Subordinate means lower in rank or importance.

In the kitchen brigade every station chef is subordinate to the executive chef, whose menu is law.

Worked Example

The hospital's chart of command is printed inside every stairwell: residents are subordinate to attending physicians, who answer to the department chief. A resident may disagree out loud — the good ones do — but once the attending decides, the resident carries it out.

Subordinate is the precise word for standing lower in a formal order: it does not call anyone less able or less valued, only lower-ranked — it is the org chart's word, not an insult.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

secondary: Secondary means second in importance — the side plot, the backup plan — whether or not any chain of command exists. Subordinate needs the chain: it places someone or something under another's formal authority. A secondary concern has no boss over it; a subordinate officer does.

inferior: Inferior says something is worse — lower in quality or worth, not merely in position. Subordinate is the org chart's word and carries no such insult: a subordinate officer may be the best soldier in the building and still rank below the colonel. Inferior judges; subordinate only locates.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

superior: the one ranked above, whose word prevails

commanding: holding the position that gives the orders

Where it sits · how far down the pecking order — junior → subordinate → menial

junior vs. subordinate: Junior is the gentlest step down — a junior partner merely arrived later and may still command plenty; subordinate states outright that another's authority stands above yours.

menial vs. subordinate: Menial sinks below subordinate: a subordinate officer still holds duties of judgment and trust, while menial work sits at the ladder's bottom — the tasks assigned when rank has run out entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — sub-

Prefix — sub-: under, below

Root — ordin

Root — ordin: order, rank

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: adjective-forming: placed, arranged

Put it together

Put it together: Sub- (under) + ordin (order, rank) + -ate (placed) = placed under, in the order of things. Latin subordinare filed people beneath one another in a chain of rank; the word still draws that chart — whoever is subordinate has someone written in above them.

Use the root in a new word: coordinate

Use the root in a new word: coordinate: The two food banks coordinate their delivery routes so no neighborhood is skipped and none is visited twice.

Word Choice

neutral / organizational

Subordinate is the org chart's adjective: it states rank and nothing else — a subordinate role, a clause subordinate to the main sentence. When contempt is wanted, this unit's noun underling supplies it; when only arrival order is meant, junior is kinder. Note the noun use too: a manager's subordinates are simply those the chart places beneath her.
